newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans bonds, price hikes to clear oil deficit.
newsitem.headline: India plans bonds, price hikes to clear oil deficit.

text.p: India is considering a mixture of moderate petroleum product price rises and bond issues to pay off a multi-billion bill to its oil companies, a senior petroleum ministry source told Reuters.
"The proposal is for a mix of bonds, or government securities, with a moderate price rise of 10-15 percent," the official said.
A proposal drawn up by top civil servants has been submitted for the United Front minority government to mull over and a cabinet decision could come any day, the source said.

The centre-left coalition's policy setting steering committee is due to meet on Thursday to discuss the often deferred steps needed to balance oil companies books and put India's oil prices back in kilter.
Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia and Petroleum Secretary Vijay L. Kelkar met on Tuesday to discuss the issue.
"It is just a proposal and needs cabinet approval," the official said, but added that the need for action was pressing and a decision was imminent after months of deferrals.

India's oil companies are owed billions of rupees for selling petroleum below market prices to support India's subsidy regime, and are desperate to be reimbursed in order to pay for feedstocks and clear loans taken to keep oil supplies moving.

Once the oil companies are repaid it could rattle the rock steady exchange rate of 35.7100 rupees to the dollar, as the companies rush for dollar loans against repaid rupee bonds in order to settle debts taken out to cover crude oil purchases.
Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Y.V. Reddy cited this as a possible reason for the rupee to lose some strength in the coming months.
Foreign exchange dealers said that could happen as early as September if the government moves swiftly.
The oil pool deficit, which tallies the debt is currently around 190 billion rupees ($5.3 billion). It stood at 155 billion rupees at the start fiscal 1997/98 on April 1.
The ministry source said the proposal calls for a 10-15 percent hike in product prices.

The price rises will exclude kerosene, the main cooking and lighting fuel of India's poor, and gasoline, which is already priced above market levels in an effective tax on car owners to subsidise the poor, is likely to escape untouched.
Diesel, which provides the greatest burden on the oil pool, is likely to rise by one rupee to 10 rupees per litre, bringing it closer to world price levels.
A ministry source said earlier this month an option to hike diesel prices 25 percent to take it out of India's administered pricing mechanism was also under consideration.

The official on Tuesday refused to comment on a report in the Economic Times daily, which said bonds would be issued to cover 90 billion rupees, or 45 percent of the outstanding bill to oil companies.
The source played down the newspaper's report that bonds could be issued to the oil companies as early as August 31.
The report said the bonds would be for maturities of three, five, seven and 10 years and would have a three-year lock in period. It said the three year paper would carry a yield around 10.3 percent.
How acceptable this recipe will be to the Petroleum Ministry and the oil companies will depend on the yield carried by the bonds and the interest rates paid by the oil companies on their loans.
They will use the bonds as collateral with banks to raise the loans, but are only likely to receive 75-80 percent of the issue price from any lender, the source said.
